metadata.methods_description: Sixty-channel scalp EEG and 4-channel EOG were recorded alongside two IMUs (forehead and exoskeleton back brace) and logged exoskeleton control signals and BMI decoder predictions. Each of nine sessions per participant had a motor imagery calibration phase without feedback, then 12 closed-loop trials in three blocks, followed by 6-minute walk and stop imagery tasks. Raw data are provided without filtering or artifact removal.

citation_details.title: Topological Bifurcation of Pre-stimulus Cortical Field Dynamics Predicts Cognitive Performance
citation_details.author: Diego Cerda Seguel
citation_details.abstract: Topological Bifurcation of Pre-stimulus Cortical Field Dynamics Predicts Cognitive Performance Abstract / Description for Zenodo (Deposit Description)This manuscript presents a large-scale computational analysis of pre-stimulus cortical dynamics and their predictive capacity for cognitive performance across three independent domains: episodic memory, motor control (exoskeleton), and perceptual decision-making. Using high-performance computing infrastructure (Patagón HPC), three public EEG datasets (ds006142, ds007788, ds002680) were processed, harmonized under the BIDS-EEG standard, encompassing a total of 48 healthy subjects and 21,524 experimental trials. Spectral variance within the beta band (13–30 Hz) was quantified in a strictly bounded temporal window spanning from −500 ms to 0 ms relative to stimulus onset (β_std). Key findings: Episodic memory (ds006142): β_std predicts memory retrieval success with AUC = 0.569 (p < 0.0001, n = 6,094 trials). Motor control (ds007788): β_std correlates with kinematic latency in exoskeleton control tasks, revealing a topological bifurcation in the population: two stable and opposite phenotypic profiles — stabilization (β_std ↓ → better performance) and controlled activation (β_std ↑ → better performance). Perceptual decision-making (ds002680): β_std correlates with reaction times in rapid visual categorization (r = 0.054, p < 0.0001, n = 9,146 valid trials). Implications: These results extend the classical Bereitschaftspotential principle (Libet et al., 1983) to non-motor domains, demonstrating that pre-stimulus cortical preparation is a transversal and predictive phenomenon. The observed phenotypic heterogeneity suggests that cognitive performance optimization can be achieved through opposite strategies of spectral modulation, challenging post-stimulus neural decoding models and opening new directions for adaptive brain-computer interfaces. citation_details.title: Phasic Intention Derivative Resilience and Multi-Lobe Cortical Reallocation During Prolonged Lower-Limb Exoskeleton Control: A 2D Source-Space Phase-Space Framework
citation_details.author: Nikil Shajan
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for lower-limb exoskeleton control suffer from severe non-stationarity during prolonged ambulation, driven by central motor fatigue and electrode impedance drift. Standard classifiers relying solely on tonic primary motor cortex (M1) band power degrade rapidly as task duration extends. Here, we introduce a two-dimensional (2D) dynamical phase-space decoding framework, [W_P(t), dW_P(t)/dt], termed the Predictive Adaptive Temporal Tracking Unit (PATTU), which combines an autoregressive source-space intention state (W_P(t)) with its first-order phasic intention derivative (dW_P(t)/dt) reconstructed via anatomically constrained standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA). Evaluated across cross-session motor imagery (EEGBCI, N=10) and prolonged lower-limb exoskeleton ambulation (ds007788, N=7), adaptive phase-space boundary tracking restores cross-session classification accuracy from 55.87% to 65.51% (+9.64%, p = 0.0078) and achieves a cohort mean held-out ROC-AUC of 0.6730 during active exoskeleton control (peaking at 0.8257 in high-responder trials, with adaptive thresholding recovering accuracy from 53.76% to 73.76% in drift-affected runs). Longitudinal source-space tracking across 40-minute exoskeleton sessions reveals that while tonic paracentral M1 source power erodes under fatigue (declining in 5 of 7 subjects; -2.30% in sub-01), the phasic intention derivative remains resilient (1.202 s⁻¹ in early alert runs vs. 1.413 s⁻¹ in late fatigued runs; 119.5% mean retention), accompanied by a +150.0 ms relative within-subject onset latency shift (45.7 ms early vs. 195.7 ms late). Cortical surface mapping across six bilateral networks demonstrates that the central nervous system preserves phasic initiation velocity by dynamically reallocating relative source power from fatigued paracentral M1 generators toward prefrontal executive (+3.59%), supplementary motor, and primary somatosensory (S1, +1.34%) hubs.
